'''''Erythronium dens-canis''''', the '''dog's-tooth-violet'''<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web |title=Dog's-tooth-violet Erythronium ''dens-canis'' L. |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.wxh |access-date=2026-04-16}}</ref> is a [[bulb]]ous [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Liliaceae. It is [[native plant|native]] to central and southern [[Europe]] from [[Portugal]] to [[Ukraine]], and locally [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] north to [[Germany]], [[Great Britain]], and [[Ireland]].<ref name="PlantAtlas"/><ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Erythronium dens-canis'' L. |website=Plants of the World Online |date=2021-04-10 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:534921-1 |access-date=2026-04-16}}</ref> It, and the closely related ''[[Erythronium caucasicum]]'' in the extreme southeast of Europe, are the only naturally occurring species of ''[[Erythronium]]'' in Europe. Despite its common name, it is not closely related to the true [[viola (plant)|violets]] of genus ''[[Viola (plant)|Viola]]''.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|page=1136}}</ref>

==Description==
''Erythronium dens-canis'' grows to {{convert|6|–|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall, flowering at the beginning of spring from February to April. The flowers are solitary, pink or lilac (rarely white), with six [[tepal]]s around 3 cm long; these are [[wikt:reflexed|reflexed]] at the top and yellow tinted at the base, and with dark purple anthers. The leaves are marbled in glaucous green and pinkish-brown or purple, and are ovate to lanceolate; they grow in pairs. The white bulb is oblong and resembles a dog's tooth, hence the common name "dog's-tooth-violet" and the Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''dens-canis'', which translates as "dog's tooth".<ref name="Huxley">{{cite book |last1=Huxley |first1=Anthony |author1-link=Anthony Huxley |title=Mountain Flowers |date=1967 |publisher=Blandford Press |location=London |page=168}}</ref><ref name="RHSD">{{cite book |last1=Huxley |first1=Anthony |title=Royal Horticultural Society Dictionary of Gardening |publisher=Macmillan Stockton press |publication-place=London New York |date=1992 |isbn=1-56159-001-0 |volume=2 |page=209}}</ref><ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|page=224}}</ref><ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358324#page/317/mode/1up Linnaeus, Carl von. 1753. Species Plantarum 1: 305.]</ref>

==Ecology==
''Erythronium dens-canis'' is found in damp, sunny or lightly shaded settings such as meadows and open woodland, mainly growing at altitudes of 500–2,000 m.<ref name="Huxley"/>

==Taxonomy==
Numerous names have been coined at [[variety (botany)|varietal]] rank for plants once considered to be included within ''Erythronium dens-canis''. None of the European varieties is now considered to merit recognition but some of the Asian species are now regarded as distinct species:<ref name=urula/>
* ''Erythronium dens-canis'' var. ''japonicum'', now called  ''[[Erythronium japonicum]]''
* ''Erythronium dens-canis'' var. ''parviflorum'', now called ''[[Erythronium sibiricum]]''
* ''Erythronium dens-canis'' var. ''sibiricum'', now called ''[[Erythronium sibiricum]]''

==Uses==
It is grown as a garden plant for its attractive flowers. It was first introduced to Britain in 1596, with naturalised plants first noted in 1965.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> <!-- AGM withdrawn It is also widely cultivated and has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Erythronium dens-canis''|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=744|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|accessdate=26 July 2013}}</ref>-->

Its leaves may be consumed raw in salad, or boiled as a leaf vegetable. The bulb is also the source of a starch used in making [[vermicelli]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Erythronium dens-canis|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Erythronium+dens-canis|work=Plants for a future|accessdate=26 July 2013}}</ref>
